description: Merge two sorted integer sequences into the existing first array. Only first[0..realCount-1] initially contains real values; its remaining slots are spare capacity. Every entry of second is real. Write the complete nondecreasing merge into first in place and return its filled values. Preserve second.
constraints: 0 <= realCount <= 5000, 0 <= second.length <= 5000, and first.length is exactly realCount+second.length. The first real prefix and all of second are independently sorted nondecreasing signed 32-bit integers. Duplicates are allowed.

The spare first-array slots may contain ANY signed values and must be ignored as input. Preserve the first array object and final length; do not allocate another merged working array. The two supplied arrays are distinct, nonnull objects. Preserve second, including its order.
C#/Java/Python/JavaScript return the filled first array; C++ returns its values by value after mutating the supplied reference. Returning a merged copy while leaving first unchanged is incorrect.
why: Merging from the front would overwrite unread values in first unless they were shifted or copied. Its unused tail is safe output space. Compare the largest unread values and place the larger at the last free output position, moving backward until second has been consumed.
correctness: Before each write, the output suffix already contains the largest consumed values in their final sorted positions. The largest unread item is at the end of one sorted input prefix, so placing that item next preserves the invariant. While second remains, the write position is strictly after the unread first prefix, so no unread first value is destroyed. When second is exhausted, any remaining first prefix is already in its correct positions. Thus first contains exactly both original sequences, in order, and second was only read.
walkthrough: For first=[1,4,7,99,99], realCount=3, second=[2,6], write 7 at index 4, then 6 at index 3, then 4 at index 2, then 2 at index 1. The untouched 1 stays at index 0, yielding [1,2,4,6,7]. The 99 placeholders are never merged.
time: O(realCount+second.length) worst-case merge time. C++ by-value return also copies that many result values, including a no-op merge.
space: O(1) auxiliary merge workspace, excluding the C++ returned value copy. No second merged working array is allocated.
edges: Either real sequence empty; both empty.
Nonzero/extreme spare values, duplicates across inputs and signed endpoints.
related: The public demonstration includes an unsorted second array; that invalid example is not used. The sorted-prefix precondition is explicit here.

description: Reorder the supplied words array in place so all words that are anagrams of one another occur in one contiguous group. Return the reordered word values as a materialized collection. Preserve every original word occurrence, including duplicates. Group order and order within a group are unrestricted.
constraints: words is a nonnull array of 0..200 nonnull strings, each 0..20 lowercase ASCII letters a..z. Words are anagrams exactly when their letter multiplicities agree. Empty strings are anagrams of one another.

Preserve the supplied array object and length; only reorder its entries. Do not deduplicate words or return groups while leaving an ungrouped input unchanged. The returned collection must equal the final words values in order.
Examples show one concrete valid ordering; the judge accepts every ordering with contiguous complete anagram groups and the original multiset.
why: Sorting the letters inside a word gives a canonical key: equal keys mean equal letter multiplicities. Compute each key once, order the decorated words by that key, then write the words back. This puts each equivalence class next to itself without changing any word or losing duplicate occurrences.
correctness: Two lowercase words have the same sorted-character key exactly when each letter occurs equally often, so key equality is precisely the anagram relation. Sorting decorated entries by key makes every equal-key class contiguous. Decoration retains one entry for each original occurrence, and writing every decorated word back preserves the complete multiset and length. Returned values mirror that final array. Ordering inside an equal-key group is irrelevant to the contract.
walkthrough: For [ate,eat,tea,bat,nat,tan], the keys are aet,aet,aet,abt,ant,ant. Ordering groups by those keys gives [bat,ate,eat,tea,nat,tan]. The three aet words form one group even though their internal letter order differs. Two copies of eat would remain two occurrences.
time: O(n*L*log(L+1) + n*L*log(n+1)) worst-case character work for n words of length at most L, including key creation and key comparisons.
space: O(n*L) auxiliary decorated/key storage; returned word references or C++ value copies are additional output storage.
edges: Empty array, empty strings and duplicate words.
Repeated letters distinguish multiplicities; anagram groups may appear in any order but may not be split.
related: This retains the public in-place grouping task; it is not an API returning nested groups without reordering the input.

languageWhy.csharp: The C# tuple array stores both each canonical key and its original word before sorting. This avoids recomputing sorted letters during comparisons and prevents writeback from overwriting an unread original word. StringComparer.Ordinal keeps key comparisons independent of locale.
languageWhy.java: Java keeps original word references in a cloned array and sorts an Integer index array by precomputed keys. Writing directly from a partly reordered input could destroy a word needed by a later index, so writeback reads the clone. Arrays.asList then supplies the already reordered values for the returned List.
languageWhy.python: Python list.sort computes its key function once per word. Sorting those keys groups anagrams without repeatedly sorting letters during comparisons. The list is changed in place; the returned copy contains the same final values and is not a substitute for mutation.
languageWhy.cpp: C++ stores key/word pairs, sorts the pairs, then copies their words back into the original vector. Pair ordering may also order words within a group, which is permitted. The returned vector is a value copy after the input has already been reordered.
languageWhy.javascript: JavaScript first decorates each word with a precomputed sorted-letter key. Sorting the decorated records avoids recomputing that key during comparisons. Copying record.word back by index preserves the original words array object; slice returns its final values afterward.

description: Search an array obtained by rotating a nondecreasing sorted array at an unknown position. Return any zero-based index containing target, or -1 if it is absent. Equal values may occur, and a zero-position rotation is allowed.
constraints: values contains 0..10000 signed 32-bit integers and has the stated rotated-sorted structure. target is any signed 32-bit integer. Preserve all input values and ordering.
When target occurs more than once, any matching index is valid; the first occurrence is not required. Empty input returns -1. Duplicate boundaries can prevent logarithmic progress.
why: Unless equal boundary/middle values obscure the pivot, at least one half is normally sorted. Its endpoint range tells whether the target can be inside it. When both boundaries equal the middle and it is not the target, discard those equal boundary items safely rather than applying an unjustified sorted-half decision.
correctness: Test the middle value before discarding anything. If left, middle and right values are equal but not the target, removing the two boundaries cannot remove a match. Otherwise a normally ordered half can be identified; target comparisons either retain that half or prove it contains no match and retain the other. This preserves every possible target occurrence in the remaining interval. Every iteration shrinks the interval, and returning -1 after it empties therefore means the target is absent. A returned index is checked directly.
walkthrough: For [4,5,6,7,0,1,2] and target 0, middle value 7 shows the left half 4..7 is sorted and cannot contain 0. Search indices 4..6, then narrow to index 4, whose value is 0. For all-equal nonmatching input, boundary trimming may require a linear scan.
time: O(log n) when distinct values permit half-interval decisions; O(n) worst case with duplicates.
space: O(1) auxiliary scalar storage in the iterative search.
edges: Empty and unrotated arrays, target absent.
Duplicate pivot values, all-equal input, multiple matching indices and signed endpoints.
related: A distinct-only binary search does not cover the public repeated-value cases.

description: Search the provided Listy without a size/length operation. Its sorted sequence contains positive integers; ElementAt(index) returns the value or -1 for an out-of-range index. Return any zero-based index containing target, or -1 when absent. Use logarithmically many ElementAt queries rather than scanning to discover the full length.
constraints: The hidden sequence has 0..10000 positive signed 32-bit integers in nondecreasing order; duplicates are allowed. target is any signed 32-bit integer. Nonpositive targets cannot occur and return -1.

The first displayed example argument describes the hidden sequence, but the callable receives Listy, not an array. Use only ElementAt(index); do not inspect a concrete subtype, underlying storage, length, or reflection. Negative indices and indices at/after the hidden end return -1.

Preserve the sequence. A case permits at most 4*ceil(log2(n+2))+8 queries, where n is its hidden length. This generous logarithmic bound admits exponential range discovery followed by binary search. Provided API declarations are visible before the solution.
why: Probe indices 1,2,4,8,... until a probe is absent or no smaller than target. The target can only lie between the preceding bound and this bound. Binary search that interval, treating -1 as beyond the end rather than as an ordinary negative value. This discovers enough range to search without first measuring the sequence.
correctness: Before each doubling, the probed value is valid and below target, so all earlier positions are also too small. When doubling stops, the target, if present, lies between half the bound and the bound: the latter is either large enough or past the hidden end. During binary search, an out-of-range or too-large value safely removes the upper part, and a smaller value removes the lower part. Equality returns a verified index. Every step shrinks the remaining interval, proving absence when it empties. Exponential discovery and binary search each use logarithmically many probes.
walkthrough: For hidden [1,2,4,5,6,7,9] and target 6, probes at 1 and 2 return 2 and 4, both too small. Probe 4 returns 6, providing an upper bound. Binary search indices 2..4 and return index 4. A -1 probe marks the end and must never match target=-1.
time: O(log(n+1)) ElementAt calls and scalar work, with constant work for a nonpositive target.
space: O(1) auxiliary indices and the latest probed value; the provided Listy storage is input, not an allocated search array.
edges: Empty and singleton sequences, nonpositive or absent targets.
Repeated values, an upper bound beyond the end, and the largest positive integer.
Linear length-discovery programs exceed the query budget on large cases.

description: Search a lexicographically sorted sequence of nonempty words with empty-string gaps inserted at arbitrary positions. Return any original-array index containing target, or -1 if absent. Empty strings are gaps, not searchable words: an empty target returns -1.
constraints: words is nonnull with 0..10000 nonnull strings, each 0..20 lowercase ASCII letters a..z. Removing its empty strings leaves a nondecreasing lexicographic sequence. target is a nonnull lowercase ASCII string of length 0..20.
Preserve the array, its gap positions and word values. Repeated nonempty words are allowed; any matching index is accepted. Comparisons use ASCII lexicographic order, consistently across languages.
why: A gap cannot determine the binary-search direction. Move outward from the midpoint to find a nearby nonempty word inside the remaining interval, then use its sorted order to discard an impossible side. If that whole interval contains only gaps, the target is absent there. Gap scans can be long, so logarithmic worst-case time is not promised.
correctness: Empty target is rejected by the explicit gap convention. For a nonempty target, finding a nonempty pivot does not change the fact that all nonempty words before it are no greater and those after it are no smaller. Comparing pivot and target therefore safely retains the only side that may contain a match, or returns the matching pivot. If no nonempty pivot exists inside the interval, no nonempty target exists there. Repeated shrinking terminates and preserves original indices without compacting the input.
walkthrough: In [at,"","",ball,"","",car,"","",dad,"",""], target ball is at index 3. The initial midpoint is a gap; scanning outward finds car at index 6, so search earlier positions. A later gap scan finds ball and returns its original index, not its index in a compacted word list.
time: O(n*(L+1)) conservative worst-case time for n positions and maximum word length L: gaps can require linear index scans and comparing words costs up to L. Dense nonempty input uses O(L*log(n+1)) time.
space: O(1) auxiliary scalar/index storage; no compacted array is created.
edges: Empty array, all gaps, and empty target.
Long gaps at endpoints or midpoint, duplicate target words and absent targets.
related: The author public wrapper also treats an empty target as not found.

description: Sort a read-only text file using external-memory runs, returning a live input/workspace TextFile whose records are in ascending ordinal order. Preserve every line occurrence, including duplicates and empty lines, and preserve the input file contents. The file can exceed the permitted record buffer: do not collect the whole input in memory. Use only the provided stream/workspace APIs; candidate code does not receive an array of all lines or direct filesystem paths.
constraints: The file contains N=0..20000 lines. Each line is 0..40 printable ASCII characters (U+0020..U+007E); line delimiters are not part of a record. Leading/trailing spaces and case are significant. The bufferLimit B is 2..1024 and is a limit on simultaneously live leased records, not a count of files. A null/None ReadLine result means EOF; an empty text line is a real record.

ReadLine returns an opaque LineRecord. CompareTo(other) gives a negative/zero/positive integer for ordinal text order. Keep at most B live records. AppendLine(record) writes its line to that file and consumes/releases that record; using it again is an error. Release explicitly discards an unused lease. All leases must be released/consumed before returning. O(ceil(N/B)) small run-file handles and fixed stream buffers are separate from the record budget.

TextWorkspace.CreateFile creates an empty disk-backed temporary file. DeleteFile accepts only a live file created by that workspace; never delete the input or directly destroy provided objects. AppendLine on the input is forbidden. Return a live input/workspace file, not a new in-memory TextFile subclass or a line array. Files remain valid after Close; Close flushes and closes stream handles, and subsequent ReadLine reopens at the beginning. Rewind also flushes pending writes and resets reading to the beginning. EOF stays EOF until Close/Rewind.

At most 16 stream handles may be open simultaneously; close completed run writers/readers before opening more. ReadLine and AppendLine calls each have a generous independent limit 8*N*(ceil(log2(max(1,N)))+2)+128, including EOF reads. At most 4*N+64 temporary files may be created. These bounds admit ordinary binary external mergesort, including one-record runs; no particular run-merging order or tie direction is required.

JSON arguments are [inputLines,bufferLimit,[]]. The judge creates the read-only input file from inputLines and injects TextFile/TextWorkspace objects; [] is the workspace placeholder. Displayed output is the returned file line sequence. Raw line text is private to the provided record comparator/writer so the live-record budget is enforced. C++ borrows provided objects/pointers; use Release/DeleteFile rather than delete.
why: Sorting only B leased records creates small sorted runs without retaining the large input. Two sorted runs can be merged while holding just their two current records: the smaller current record must be the next output because everything behind either cursor is at least that cursor value. Writing consumes that lease, leaving room to read its successor. Repeated pairwise merging reduces the run count until one complete sorted file remains.
correctness: Every chunk is a disjoint consecutive part of the input, and sorting changes only its order. Writing the chunk therefore creates a sorted run with exactly those occurrences. For a merge, maintain that the output is sorted and contains exactly the consumed prefixes of both runs. Choosing the smaller current record extends this output in sorted order; once a run ends, the other remaining sorted suffix can be copied. Thus the merged run is sorted and preserves the union multiset. Carrying an unpaired run unchanged preserves the same invariant. Each merge round reduces the number of runs, so termination leaves one sorted run containing all input occurrences. Empty input returns an empty workspace file. Chunk writing consumes all B-or-fewer leases before merging; each merge keeps at most two current leases, so B>=2 suffices.
walkthrough: With B=2 and lines [pear,"",apple,pear," A",a], the sorted chunks are ["",pear], [apple,pear] and [" A",a]. Merge the first two: compare the two current records, write the smaller, then read a replacement from that same file; the result is ["",apple,pear,pear]. Carry the third run into the next round. Their merge produces [""," A",a,apple,pear,pear]. Both pear occurrences survive. Each append consumes its current record, so the merge never holds more than two live records, and the leading space is preserved.
time: For R=ceil(N/B) nonempty initial runs, chunk sorting takes O(N log B) comparisons and merging O(N log(max(1,R))) comparisons. ASCII line length is bounded; otherwise comparator cost includes compared text length. Disk traffic is O(N*(1+log(max(1,R)))) records. Empty input takes O(1) file operations.
space: At most B live record payloads, plus O(R) small run-file handles and fixed stream buffers. The reference stores no full input/result array. Live scratch-file contents occupy O(N) records because consumed runs are deleted. The judge projection/lease instrumentation is separate from candidate working storage.
edges: No lines, one line, empty lines versus EOF, duplicate lines and all-equal input.
Ordinal case/space/prefix order, odd run counts and partial final chunks.
B=2, B>=N, 20000 input lines and bounded live record payloads.
Consumed-record reuse, read-only input, foreign/deleted output files and stream/file I/O limits.
related: The author-linked chapter-10 public source describes splitting a large file into runs and repeatedly merging files. This callable uses disk-backed opaque comparable records to enforce a scalable record-count memory budget. It remains an external-file sorting exercise rather than substituting an in-memory array sort.

languageWhy.csharp: C# sorts a List<LineRecord> with a CompareTo lambda, writes/consumes every chunk lease, and keeps TextFile references only for run metadata. Null EOF checks are separate from record comparisons. Explicit Close calls bound open streams; null-forgiving annotations in the merge are justified by its nonempty-head invariant.
languageWhy.java: Java ArrayList<LineRecord> sorting uses the provided comparator, not raw text or locale collation. A pair of nullable record references represents stream heads. Each written head is consumed before ReadLine obtains its successor; run files are closed and deleted only after their contents reach the merged file.
languageWhy.cpp: C++ vectors contain borrowed LineRecord*/TextFile* handles, with protected base destructors preventing direct deletion. Comparator lambdas dereference only live record pointers; AppendLine consumes a record. The workspace owns file lifetimes, and temporary files are removed through DeleteFile after each merge.
languageWhy.python: Python cmp_to_key wraps the provided comparator for a bounded record list. is None identifies EOF without confusing it with an empty line. The list contains record handles, and appending each record consumes its lease before the next phase; only run-file metadata survives the chunk phase.
languageWhy.javascript: JavaScript sorts each bounded array with the provided CompareTo comparator rather than default object-string sorting. Explicit null checks implement EOF. Each append consumes one head before replacing it, while closing writers/readers keeps disk handles bounded.

title: Sort Big File

csharp.signature: TextFile SortExternalFile(TextFile inputFile, int bufferLimit, TextWorkspace workspace)

python.signature: def SortExternalFile(inputFile: TextFile, bufferLimit: int, workspace: TextWorkspace) -> TextFile
python.starterCode:
def SortExternalFile(inputFile: TextFile, bufferLimit: int, workspace: TextWorkspace) -> TextFile:
    return inputFile
python.solutionCode:
def SortExternalFile(inputFile: TextFile, bufferLimit: int, workspace: TextWorkspace) -> TextFile:
    from functools import cmp_to_key

    inputFile.Rewind()
    runs = []
    while True:
        chunk = []
        for _ in range(bufferLimit):
            record = inputFile.ReadLine()
            if record is None:
                break
            chunk.append(record)
        if not chunk:
            break
        chunk.sort(key=cmp_to_key(lambda first, second: first.CompareTo(second)))
        run = workspace.CreateFile()
        for record in chunk:
            run.AppendLine(record)
        run.Close()
        runs.append(run)
    inputFile.Close()
    if not runs:
        empty = workspace.CreateFile()
        empty.Close()
        return empty
    while len(runs) > 1:
        merged = []
        for index in range(0, len(runs), 2):
            if index + 1 == len(runs):
                merged.append(runs[index])
                continue
            left, right = runs[index], runs[index + 1]
            left.Rewind()
            right.Rewind()
            output = workspace.CreateFile()
            first, second = left.ReadLine(), right.ReadLine()
            while first is not None or second is not None:
                if second is None or first is not None and first.CompareTo(second) <= 0:
                    output.AppendLine(first)
                    first = left.ReadLine()
                else:
                    output.AppendLine(second)
                    second = right.ReadLine()
            output.Close()
            left.Close()
            right.Close()
            workspace.DeleteFile(left)
            workspace.DeleteFile(right)
            merged.append(output)
        runs = merged
    runs[0].Rewind()
    return runs[0]

description: Find ANY absent integer in the full nonnegative signed-32-bit domain 0..2147483647 from a readonly integer file. The provided NumberFile initially points to its first value. ReadNext() returns the next integer, or -1 at end of file. Reset() rewinds to the first value. Implement both memory modes: smallMemory=false permits a one-pass bitmap using up to 1 GiB of auxiliary storage; smallMemory=true permits up to 10 MiB and two passes, and additionally guarantees distinct file values.
constraints: The file contains 0..2147483647 values, each in 0..2147483647, so at least one domain value is absent. Repetitions are allowed only when smallMemory=false. The returned integer must be absent; the smallest absent value is not required.

The callable receives NumberFile, not an array or ranges. Example/test wire storage is an array of inclusive integer ranges [[start,end],...]; the judge lazily streams every value of each range in order, including repeated values from overlapping/repeated ranges in full-memory mode. Each range is nonempty and within the domain. In small-memory mode ranges cannot overlap. The expanded file length obeys the stated bound.

ReadNext has constant cost and returns -1 persistently after EOF until Reset. With full memory, do not Reset and use at most length+1 reads; with small memory, at most one Reset and 2*(length+1) reads. File contents are readonly. Do not inspect private backing storage or retain a file-sized list/set of values; memory budgets concern algorithm storage beyond the supplied stream and language runtime.

A domain bitmap has exactly 2^31 bits = 268435456 bytes and fits the 1 GiB mode. The small-memory mode must avoid that allocation. Its distinct-value promise matters: bucket COUNTS do not prove all values in a bucket are present when duplicates are allowed.
why: For full memory, one bit per possible integer records presence regardless of repetitions. A zero bit identifies an absent value. With only 10 MiB, first count values in each 2^20-sized block. Distinct values make a block count below 2^20 proof that it has a missing member. Rewind and record only that block in a 2^20-bit bitmap, reducing bitmap storage to 131072 bytes.
correctness: In full mode, processing v sets exactly its presence bit and never clears a bit. After the pass, a zero bit is therefore equivalent to absence; fewer than 2^31 file entries guarantees one exists. In small mode, every integer belongs to exactly one of 2048 blocks. Since values are distinct, each count equals the number of present values in that block. At least one count is below its capacity, so the selected block contains an absent value. On the second pass only values whose high block bits match the chosen block set local presence bits. A zero local bit therefore denotes a truly absent domain value. The block-index comparison avoids overflowing an exclusive upper endpoint for the highest block. Neither proof applies to a repeated-value bucket count without the distinctness promise.
walkthrough: A file represented by [[0,2],[4,4]] streams 0,1,2,4. Full mode sets those four bits and finds missing 3. In small mode block 0 has count 4<1048576; after Reset, its local bitmap again identifies 3. If [[0,1048575]] is the whole file, block 0 is full, so the small-memory search chooses block 1 and returns 1048576. A file containing 2147483647 must not overflow its stream cursor or last bitmap index.
time: Full mode O(N+U/8) worst-case byte scanning plus fixed eight-bit inspection per nonfull byte; small mode O(N+B+R/8), where U=2^31, B=2048 and R=2^20. The file is streamed once or twice, not expanded into a local array.
space: Full mode exactly U/8=268435456 bitmap bytes plus O(1) state. Small mode 131072 bitmap bytes plus 2048 counters and O(1) state; even language object overhead for the counters stays well below 10 MiB. Supplied stream storage is excluded.
edges: Empty file, duplicate values in full mode and arbitrary file order.
All values of the first block present, a missing interior value, and maximum signed value present.
No integer overflow at 2^31, sticky EOF, one rewind and the distinctness-only count proof.
related: The public implementations search a file over the nonnegative Java-int domain using either a complete bitmap or block counts plus a smaller bitmap. This binding makes the memory modes, missing-value guarantee, stream API and low-memory distinctness assumption explicit rather than replacing the file with an ordinary set lookup.

description: Report every occurrence of an integer after its first occurrence, in original encounter order. For example, three occurrences of 8 contribute two returned 8s. All values lie in 1..32000, and the actual largest value is not supplied. Preserve the input and use the interview's 4KB marking workspace.
constraints: values is a nonnull array of 0..10000 integers in 1..32000. Return a concrete integer array/list/vector of repeated occurrences; do not deduplicate the output or sort the input.

Use at most 4000 bytes of marking bits and constant scalar bookkeeping. Input, final returned storage and language/runtime object headers are excluded from this logical 4KB interview workspace budget. A hash set or one-byte-per-value table does not meet the marking budget.

The implementation may read the array more than once. Count repeated occurrences first, then reuse the same bitmap to fill an exactly sized result, avoiding a separate growing output buffer plus a final copied array.
why: One bit records whether a value has appeared, so 32000 possible values need 32000/8=4000 bytes. Subtract one before choosing the byte and bit because values begin at one. Returning an array instead of printing requires its size; a counting pass and a second pass with the cleared same bitmap avoid an extra input-sized working collection.
correctness: During either pass, the bit for a value is set exactly when that value has appeared earlier in that pass. A clear bit is set on first occurrence; a set bit therefore identifies precisely each later occurrence. The first pass counts exactly the output length. Clearing all bitmap bytes restores the initial invariant, and the second pass writes those same repeated encounters into the preallocated result in input order. No input value is changed, every repeat is included and no first occurrence is included.
walkthrough: For [8,1,8,8,32000,32000], the first 8 sets bit 7 of byte 0. Its next two occurrences are both repeats. The first 32000 sets the final bitmap bit; its next occurrence repeats. Count three outputs, clear the bitmap, and fill [8,8,32000] on the second pass.
time: O(n+U/8) time for two scans and clearing U/8 marking bytes, where U=32000 is fixed; hence O(n+1) for this domain.
space: 4000 marking bytes plus O(1) scalar bookkeeping, excluding the exactly sized final result. The bitmap is reused, not doubled between passes.
edges: Empty input, all distinct values and one value repeated many times.
Values 1,8,9,31999,32000 cross byte and signed-byte boundaries.
Output multiplicity is occurrence count minus one, not one per distinct duplicate value.
related: The author public code prints each repeated encounter; this callable returns that same sequence under an explicit memory model.
title: Find Duplicates

description: Find target in a rectangular integer matrix whose rows and columns are each nondecreasing. Return any matching [row,column] coordinate using zero-based indices, or [-1,-1] when absent. Rows need not form one globally sorted flattened sequence.
constraints: matrix is nonnull, rectangular, with 0..50 rows and 0..50 columns. All entries and target are signed 32-bit integers. Duplicate values are allowed. Preserve outer/row objects and all values.
Either empty dimension has no match. Any valid target coordinate is accepted when several exist. Do not assume the last value of one row is below the first value of the next row.
why: At the top-right remaining cell, everything below it is at least as large and everything to its left is no larger. A value above target rules out that entire column; a value below target rules out that entire row. This staircase walk removes one row or column per comparison.
correctness: Initially every possible target position is in the full remaining rectangle. If its top-right value is larger than target, all values below in that column are also too large, so removing the column is safe. If smaller, all remaining values in that row are too small, so removing the row is safe. Equality returns a verified coordinate. This invariant preserves every possible match until the rectangle empties, proving the [-1,-1] result then means absence.
walkthrough: For [[1,4,7],[2,5,8],[3,6,9]] and target 6, begin at 7 and move left to 4. Move down to 5, then down to 6, returning [2,1]. Flattened binary search would be invalid because 7 at the end of row 0 exceeds 2 at the start of row 1.
time: O(rows+columns) comparisons, since each step removes one row or column.
edges: Empty dimensions, one row or column, target outside the value range.
Duplicates, signed endpoints and row ranges that overlap.

description: Implement RankTracker for a stream of integers. Track(value) records one occurrence. GetRank(value) returns the number of tracked occurrences less than or equal to value, excluding ONE occurrence of value itself. Other equal occurrences still count. Return -1 if value has never been tracked, including an empty tracker.
constraints: The input transcript has 1..2001 operations. The first is RankTracker with []; every later operation is Track or GetRank with exactly one signed 32-bit integer. Construct a fresh tracker for each transcript.

Track returns no value, represented by null in results. Constructor output is also null. Return one result per operation in order. GetRank returns a zero-based last-occurrence rank among sorted tracked values; an absent query returns -1, not the insertion position.
Preserve transcript inputs. Support changing stream state and duplicates; do not sort the caller transcript. Private implementation nodes are not caller-provided models.
why: A search-tree node can cache how many tracked occurrences lie in its left subtree. Route equal inserted values left, so that count also includes earlier/later duplicates beneath an equal node. A rank query accumulates entire left subtrees and ancestor nodes only when moving right; finding the queried value adds its left count without counting that node itself.
correctness: Every insertion preserves the BST rule left<=node<right and increments a node's left count exactly when the new occurrence enters that left subtree. During a query, the accumulated count contains exactly the smaller/equal occurrences already skipped on right turns. At equality, every left-subtree occurrence is <=value, and the current node is the one excluded occurrence, so accumulated+leftCount is the required rank. If traversal reaches no matching node, the value is absent and -1 is returned regardless of the partial accumulated count. Iterative traversal avoids recursion-depth failures on a skewed stream.
walkthrough: Track 5,1,4,4. Sorted tracked values are [1,4,4,5]. GetRank(4) returns 2: one 1 and the OTHER 4 count, while one queried 4 is excluded. GetRank(2) returns -1 even though its insertion position would be 1. A new tracker begins empty.
time: O(h) per Track/GetRank for tree height h. The actual BST is not balanced: worst-case h equals the number of tracked occurrences; do not claim guaranteed logarithmic time.
space: O(t) stored nodes after t tracked occurrences and O(1) auxiliary iterative traversal space, excluding the returned transcript results.
edges: Query before any Track and query an absent interior value.
Repeated equal values count other copies; negative and signed-endpoint values.
Ascending/descending streams create skewed trees but not recursive stack overflow.
related: A fresh class replaces the public static root; rank semantics match its node left-size definition and explicit absence result.

description: Reorder values in place so every odd zero-based position is a peak: its value is at least each existing adjacent neighbor. Consequently even positions are valleys. Equal neighbors are allowed. Return the final values; any arrangement satisfying this pattern and preserving the original multiset is accepted.
constraints: values is a nonnull array of 0..10000 signed 32-bit integers. Preserve its original array object and length; only reorder entries. Empty and singleton arrays already satisfy the pattern.

Use O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary rearrangement storage. Do not sort the full array. C#/Java/Python/JavaScript return the same array; C++ returns a value copy after mutating the reference. Returning a different valid arrangement while leaving an invalid input unchanged is incorrect.
why: For each odd position, put the largest value among it and its existing neighbors at that position. It then dominates both neighbors. If the left neighbor is swapped, it receives a value no greater than its old value, so it cannot break the previous peak. This permits a single local pass instead of sorting.
correctness: After processing an odd position, it is at least both adjacent values by construction. The only cell shared with the preceding processed triple is its left neighbor. If that neighbor is chosen as the new peak, the displaced center is no larger than the old neighbor, so the previous peak still dominates it; other swaps do not change that shared neighbor. Induction therefore preserves all earlier peaks. Every odd position is processed, so the final array has the full alternating pattern. Swaps alone preserve every original occurrence.
walkthrough: Starting with [1,2,3,4,5], put 3 at odd index 1 by swapping it with 2, giving [1,3,2,4,5]. Then swap 5 into odd index 3, yielding [1,3,2,5,4]. Both peaks dominate their neighbors; the middle valley 2 is below both 3 and 5.
time: O(n) time for one constant-work step per odd position; the C++ returned copy is also O(n).
space: O(1) auxiliary rearrangement storage, excluding the C++ returned value copy.
edges: Empty, singleton, equal values and two-element arrays.
Signed extremes must not be confused with out-of-bounds sentinels.
Multiple valid outputs are accepted, but all input occurrences must remain.
related: The explicit odd-peak orientation follows the author public local-maximum variant; a merely sorted output does not satisfy the task.
title: Peaks and Valleys

description: Read the text file at filePath and return its last k lines in their original order. If it contains fewer than k lines, return every line. Return line contents without their line terminators; an empty line is a real line, not end of file. Preserve the file. This callable returns the lines instead of printing them so the judge can compare the requested output.
constraints: k is an integer in 1..1000. The judge supplies an existing readable file containing 0..20000 lines. Each line contains 0..128 printable ASCII characters (codes 32..126), followed by LF. The empty file contains zero lines. The final LF terminates the last line; it does not create an additional empty line. File opening and reading succeed for admitted inputs.

The first JSON argument is an array of line contents. The judge writes those lines to an actual temporary file and passes its path to LastKLines; your callable receives a path string, not that array. The second argument is k. Do not change or remove the file, and close any stream you open before returning.

Process the file sequentially, retaining at most k complete lines plus bounded read buffers and one current line. Do not load the entire file. Return a concrete sequence of strings. The return sequence may use O(k) references; returned character storage depends on the retained line lengths.
why: A line can only belong to the final answer until k later lines arrive. Keeping a bounded queue therefore discards exactly the lines that have become too old. It avoids reading the whole file into memory and handles files shorter than k without padding. The final queue already has the required chronological order.
correctness: After processing t lines, the queue contains exactly the last min(t,k) processed lines in their original order. Initially this is true for the empty queue. Append the next line; if there are now k+1 entries, removing the oldest leaves exactly the most recent k. Otherwise all processed lines still fit. This proves the invariant by induction. At end of file, the queue is the required suffix. Testing the read operation for EOF rather than testing whether its string is empty preserves empty lines. No write operation is performed on the input file.
walkthrough: For a file with lines [north,"",east,west,south] and k=3, the queue evolves [north], [north,""], [north,"",east], ["",east,west], then [east,west,south]. The fourth and fifth reads discard only the oldest retained line. The output is [east,west,south]. For a file containing one blank line, the result is [""]; an empty file returns [].
time: O(N + C) time, where N is the number of lines and C is the number of file characters read. Each line enters and leaves the bounded queue at most once; constructing the result touches at most k entries.
space: O(k + S + B) space, where S is the total character storage of the retained lines and B is the fixed read buffer plus one line being assembled. With the admitted 128-character line limit this is O(k) auxiliary/output storage. The entire file is never retained.
edges: Empty file, one blank line, blank lines within the final suffix, and whitespace-only lines.
k=1, k larger than the line count, exactly k lines, and multiple circular-buffer wraps.
20000 lines, maximum line length, punctuation and case preserved exactly; file contents preserved.
related: The author-linked C++ print_k_lines implementation establishes sequential last-k file output; the independent course index identifies it as 12.1. Its stopping-on-empty-line behavior is not adopted: this bank explicitly treats blank lines as lines and uses actual EOF. All five independent implementations retain a bounded suffix and close their streams.

languageWhy.csharp: C# File.ReadLines reads lazily. Queue<string> retains the suffix, and foreach disposes its enumerator, closing the file before ToList returns the concrete result.
languageWhy.java: Java BufferedReader reads one line at a time. ArrayDeque removes its oldest entry in constant amortized time; try-with-resources closes the reader even if a read fails. The admitted inputs guarantee successful I/O; an unexpected IOException is reported rather than silently returning a partial suffix.
languageWhy.cpp: C++ std::getline distinguishes a successfully read empty line from EOF. std::deque supports constant-time removal at the front; the local ifstream closes through RAII when the method returns.
languageWhy.python: Python imports deque inside the callable, then iterates an open file inside a with block and strips exactly the terminating LF from each admitted line. deque(maxlen=k) automatically discards the oldest entry. The with block closes the file before list materializes the final suffix; the deque already owns the retained strings.
languageWhy.javascript: JavaScript requires the built-in node:fs module inside the callable and uses synchronous readSync with a fixed 4096-byte buffer, not readFileSync. Printable ASCII makes byte-to-character decoding unambiguous. A k-slot circular array overwrites the oldest line; the output starts at the oldest retained slot. finally closes the descriptor, including unexpected failures.
